accuracy.evidence: Follows Common Core L.1.5 closely: sorting words into categories (L.1.5a), defining by category and one or more key attributes with the standard's own duck and tiger examples (L.1.5b) and real-life connections such as cozy places at home (L.1.5c). Facts in the cards were checked: swans and penguins swim, owls hoot, lions have manes, cheetahs have spots and only the tiger has stripes, so each definition fits exactly one card.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips teachers report with early definitions: a category that is too broad ('a thing', 'something'), an attribute every member shares ('has wings', 'has fur' rejected because the count does not drop), a false attribute ('four legs' rejected), a sometimes-true attribute ('a hat is red'), defining by a single example ('like my blue one') and circular definitions ('a spoon is a spoon').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdefine uses a live sentence strip and a grid of picture cards that fade and cross out as the definition narrows, with a 'Fits N of M' counter, which no other English lab has. Its steps (group chip, attribute chips, word book, three-bin sort, cozy home scene) differ from the sorting labs flagsort and flagsortw, and the shingle gate stayed under 30 percent against every flag file.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees why a category comes first when 'a thing' leaves every card alight and 'a bird' fades the cat, fish and car. Adding 'that swims' still leaves three birds, so the need for a key attribute is discovered rather than told, and 'that quacks' finishes it. The fix step then contrasts good and weak definitions, and the cozy scene ties the word to lived experience.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions carry real temptation: choosing 'a thing' versus 'a bird' as the group for duck, and believing 'a bird that swims' fits only the duck. The fading cards and the counter that stays at three disprove the wrong option immediately, and the done message echoes the prediction back through A.reveal.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions cover category, key attribute, sometimes-true attributes, sorting and real-life links, and nine tagged wrong-answer messages (broad, self, done, short, fine, tool, cloth, cold, loud) each explain the specific slip, for example that lions are big cats too so the tiger definition is not finished. A streak counter follows correct answers.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores below grade 1 on Flesch-Kincaid with one idea per sentence and the duck, tiger, spoon and hat examples reused across text and lab. Adult text sits near grade 5 to 6 while still naming category, key attribute and real-life connection exactly as the standard does. Card labels are single words beside a large emoji.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph adds one step of the method (group, attribute, true and specific, no circular words, real life). Adult paragraphs give the standards, the terms, the common mistakes and the lab map without repetition. Every practice and mastery item asks the child to apply the method to a new word or count how many cards a definition fits.

mobile.evidence: The lab uses the 'young' class so buttons are large, chips wrap to two rows on narrow screens and two-line text wrapping keeps sentences inside the strip. The browser gate completed every Show me on the iPhone 13 profile, and every drag (group chips, attribute chips, definition rows, sort card) has a matching button in the control row.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reported no violations in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13. The canvas aria-label mirrors every spoken result, crossed-out cards also fade and the counter states the number left, so colour is never the only signal. All controls are native buttons with descriptive aria-labels such as 'Add: that quacks'.
